Apulia
uh-PYOO-lee-uh
n. (the region of the Italian heel, holding Greek-rite villages and Waldensian colonies until the suppression of 1561)
From Latin Apulia, the land of the Apuli, an Italic people of the south-east.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Apulia is the long region of the Italian heel, a country of olive plains, limestone and harbours facing Greece. Two things set it apart in church history. It kept Greek-rite Christian villages for centuries after the rest of the peninsula was Latin, a legacy of Byzantine rule, with Greek liturgy and married clergy surviving in pockets into the modern period; the Latinisation of those parishes was pressed from the sixteenth century onward. And it held colonies of Waldenses who had migrated from the Alpine valleys in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries into Apulia and Calabria, farming settlements that kept their own barbes, their own books and a quiet separation from the parish. In 1559 and 1560 those colonies were discovered to have openly joined the Reformed churches; in 1561 the viceroy of Naples and the Inquisition destroyed them, with massacres, galley sentences and forced dispersal. The dictionary records Apulia for both: a region that preserved an older Christianity that Rome eventually suppressed, and that sheltered a confessing people whose end was violent and almost entirely forgotten.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a colony as a body of people settled in a distant country; a rite as the form of a religious ceremony; dispersion as the act of scattering; a remnant as that which is left; and suppression as the act of putting down.

expand to see more

COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country to cultivate and inhabit it.

RITE, n. The manner of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept or custom; a formal act of religion.

DISPERSION, n. The act of scattering; the state of being scattered or separated into remote parts.

REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.

SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, crushing or putting an end to; the act of concealing or keeping back.

Modern Corruption

Region of the Italian heel which kept Greek-rite villages and Waldensian farming colonies until the suppression of 1561 under the viceroy of Naples.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the quiet erasure of a confessing people, which is a different crime from the famous massacres and is easier to commit. The Apulian and Calabrian Waldenses had lived for a century or more as farmers who paid their rents and kept their own teachers, and when they identified themselves publicly with the Reformed churches they were destroyed in a single season and left almost no record. John sees such people and gives their deaths a location that no archive can take away: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the doctrine of the remnant. Scripture insists repeatedly that God keeps a small number when the visible body has gone over, and it treats that number as his doing rather than theirs: “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). Isaiah says what would have happened without it, “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9), and Hebrews gives the verdict on the hunted that the world never gives them: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38). A colony of farmers in the heel of Italy is exactly the sort of thing the dictionary exists to keep from being lost twice.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew she'ar (H7605), a remnant; Greek leimma (G3005), a remnant; Greek martyria (G3141), testimony.

expand to see more

Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant, that which is left over; “there is a remnant according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Greek ekloge (G1589) — a choosing out, election; “according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Hebrew sarid (H8300) — a survivor, one left remaining; “had left unto us a very small remnant”, Isaiah 1:9.

Greek psuche (G5590) — soul, life; “the souls of them that were slain for the word of God”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek axios (G0514) — worthy, of weight; “Of whom the world was not worthy”, Hebrews 11:38.

Usage

"“the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — where the Apulian colonies are seen."

"“there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — why a small body is not a failed one."

"“Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — the verdict the archives do not record."
